# Bengaluru triple-murder co-accused used AI tool to plan killings, cops say, seek chat history

## In what could be India's first hi-tech murder, police say Kenneth quizzed the AI chatbot with hypothetical queries over 6 months; they now probe details

The Federal  
22 July 2026 3:49 PM IST

Click the Play button to hear this message in audio format

The probe into the spine-chilling triple murder case in Bengaluru in June has seen a fresh revelation. It has been found that one of the accused, Kenneth, took the help of a unique confidant to execute the murders — those of the parents and the sister of his live-in partner and the other accused Shwetha — an AI chatbot, constituting perhaps the first of its kind case in the country. Both the accused are techies.

The city police have contacted the AI tool’s parent firm to know details of the chat history after their investigation unearthed that artificial intelligence was being used to make the sinister plan over almost six months, official sources said on Tuesday (July 21).

## Taking help of Google Gemini

*India Today* cited the police telling it that Kenneth relied on Google Gemini to prepare his dangerous plan. It was also revealed that he had planned initially to use an iron furnace to get rid of the bodies. But on consulting the chatbot and weighing in other logistical issues, he allegedly decided against it.

Police also said that Kenneth allegedly avoided asking the chatbot explicitly about how to commit a murder or how to dispose of a body. Instead, he chose to present hypothetical scenarios, framing his queries like if something had happened on those lines, what options did he have.

Bengaluru Police reportedly wrote to Google requesting access to the history of Kenneth’s engagement with the AI tool.

## Killings took place on June 22 at Shwetha-Kenneth's house

The ghastly killings took place at a rented apartment in Seegahalli in eastern Bengaluru, where 52-year-old Somasundar, his 48-year-old wife Muthulaxmi and their teenage younger daughter Supriya were stabbed to death. Shwetha, 24, is the couple's elder daughter.

She fled the scene with Kenneth after the crime, and the duo was arrested separately from Puducherry, a few days later.

Initial probe revealed that the alleged motive that led to the murders seemed to be financial disputes and strained relations between Shwetha and her family members. During interrogation, she accused her family of controlling her life, police said.

The dispute worsened after Swetha allegedly failed to pay off a bank loan and notices started knocking on her parents’ doors. Somasundar and Muthulaxmi were also not happy with her relations with Kenneth. It was when her parents and sister went to the live-in couple’s residence to confront them that the attacks took place.

The police said that after luring Muthulaxmi to their apartment on the fateful day, Kenneth stabbed her multiple times. Subsequently, when her husband and younger daughter arrived, they too were attacked fatally.

Somasundar managed to reach the staircase despite his grievous injuries. He was noticed by neighbours, who alerted the police. In his dying declaration, he told police that he had been stabbed by his daughter and her live-in partner and urged them to rescue his wife and younger daughter before he was taken to hospital, where he later died.

## Kenneth confesses to using AI

Kenneth told the police during interrogation that it was a trivial matter that led him to eliminate Shwetha’s family members. He conceded that he banked on the AI chatbot to guide him through a six-month plan to carry out the mission, the police said. The police subsequently wrote to Google to corroborate his version.

Meanwhile, psychological assessments conducted during the probe revealed that Kenneth suffered from severe social isolation. Police alleged that Shwetha financially supported Kenneth while he remained socially isolated from friends and family.

Police said Shwetha had earlier worked in the IT sector but lost her job after allegedly becoming increasingly influenced by Kenneth.

After the murders, the accused duo allegedly went to Shwetha's house, from where they stole cash and silver ornaments before fleeing to Puducherry, they said.

# Bengaluru triple murder: Accused allegedly used AI chatbot to plan killings, police say

## During interrogation, Kenneth allegedly told police that the idea of disposing of the bodies using an iron furnace came after consulting the AI tool. Police said Kenneth had built the furnace as part of plans to start a cloud kitchen but later considered using it for dispose of the bodies.

Written by : TNM Staff

Published:20th Jul, 2026 at 9:18 AM

Bengaluru police investigating a triple murder in the city found that one of the accused allegedly used a popular artificial intelligence (AI) chatbot over several months to plan the crime, including seeking information on methods of killing, disposing of bodies and removing bloodstains. The police have sought the accused's chat records from the chatbot's parent company as part of the digital evidence in the case, according to The Indian Express.

The accused, 25-year-old engineer Kenneth, and his live-in partner, Shwetha Somasundar (25), were arrested by the KR Puram police for the alleged murders of Shwetha's mother, Muthulakshmi S. (48), father, Somasundar (54), and younger sister, Supriya (20). The three were allegedly killed at the couple's apartment in K R Puram on June 22.

According to The Indian Express, Kenneth allegedly consulted the AI chatbot over nearly six months while planning the murders. Police said they have written to the chatbot's parent company seeking complete logs of his conversations to corroborate other digital evidence collected during the investigation.

During interrogation, Kenneth allegedly told police that the idea of disposing of the bodies using an iron furnace came after consulting the AI tool. Police said Kenneth had built the furnace as part of plans to start a cloud kitchen but later considered using it for disposal of the bodies.

"He was planning to start a cloud kitchen and had built an iron furnace for this purpose. When the idea of murder came up, he consulted the AI tool, which indicated the merits and demerits of incinerating bodies before disposal. He planned to repurpose the furnace," a police source said.

Police said the alleged motive behind the murders appears to be linked to financial disputes and strained family relations. Police sources said both accused come from middle-class families. Kenneth's father is a retired employee of a defence public sector undertaking involved in aircraft manufacturing, while Shwetha's late father worked for a multinational IT company.

Investigators said psychological assessments conducted during the probe pointed to severe social isolation. According to police, Shwetha had earlier worked in a high-paying role at a multinational social media company but lost her job after becoming increasingly dependent on Kenneth.

Police described their relationship as transactional, alleging that Shwetha financially supported Kenneth while he remained socially isolated from friends and family.

**Background of the case**

On June 22, police alleged, Muthulakshmi was lured to the K R Puram apartment, where Kenneth stabbed her 26 times. When Shwetha's father and younger sister arrived separately a short while later, they too were allegedly attacked and killed.

After the murders, the couple allegedly travelled to Shwetha's parental home in southeast Bengaluru and stole cash and silver ornaments before fleeing to Puducherry. Police said they had also travelled to Puducherry on vacation about two weeks before the killings.

The investigation gathered momentum after Somasundar, despite sustaining fatal injuries, managed to crawl out of the apartment. Neighbours found him on the staircase around 9 pm. Before succumbing to his injuries, he reportedly gave a dying declaration identifying his daughter Shwetha and Kenneth as the attackers and urged police to rescue his wife and younger daughter, who remained inside the flat.

Shwetha was arrested in Puducherry on June 24, while Kenneth was arrested within the following two days.

Shwetha was remanded to judicial custody on July 10 after the completion of her police custody. Police said she has expressed willingness to make a confessional statement in exchange for a pardon. Kenneth, who underwent polygraph and other scientific examinations during nine days of police custody, was remanded to judicial custody by a Bengaluru magistrate court on Saturday, July 18.

# 6 months, a plan to kill & an AI tool: What police found in Bengaluru triple murder

## The alleged motive, according to case records: a dispute over money Shwetha had taken from her parents to spend on her partner.

Shwetha was arrested in Puducherry on June 24, two days after the murders of her parents and sister, and Kenneth within the next two days (Express photo/Special arrangement).

Written by: Johnson T.A.

6 min read*Bengaluru*Jul 21, 2026 06:59 AM IST  
First published on: Jul 21, 2026 at 05:05 AM IST

* Make us preferred source on Google

He planned the murders for six months.

At every step, he turned to a trusted source for answers: how to kill three people; which chemicals could remove bloodstains; how to package the bodies; how to move them out of the apartment; how to fend off anyone who intruded into the house; and whether the furnace he had built for a planned cloud kitchen in Bengaluru could be repurposed to incinerate the bodies before disposal.

Advertisement

That trusted source, according to police and court records, was an AI tool linked to a popular search engine — a discovery, a police officer said, that left investigators so stunned they “almost considered naming the AI tool as an accomplice”.

Case records show the sequence of events came to a head on June 25, when Bengaluru police arrested Kenneth (25) and his live-in partner Shwetha, both engineering graduates who had been planning to start a business, for allegedly killing her mother Muthulakshmi S (48), sister Supriya (20) and father Somasundar (54), in that order, at their flat in K R Puram three days earlier. The alleged motive, according to case records: a dispute over money Shwetha had taken from her parents to spend on her partner.

This is possibly the first time Bengaluru police have encountered such extensive use of an AI tool in the planning and execution of a murder, sources familiar with the probe said. The tool allegedly shaped Kenneth’s thinking at every stage and had a significant bearing on how the crime was planned, they said.

Advertisement

So much so, as part of the investigation, police have written to the AI tool’s makers seeking details of Kenneth’s interactions with it, to corroborate the digital evidence in the case.

For investigators, the case also points to the social isolation of a tech-savvy generation immersed in the information and entertainment served up by their devices. “The girl did not have any friend, male or female, other than Kenneth from her college days. Kenneth had a girlfriend earlier who left him because she suspected him of lying and stealing,” sources said.

Kenneth’s alleged inability to reflect on the consequences of his actions, a lack of social responsibility, and a rapid build-up of frustration that led to an “eliminate them” mindset, “as though life were a video game”, were among the other factors behind the crime, police sources said.

Last Saturday, a magistrate’s court remanded Kenneth to judicial custody after nine days in police custody, during which police conducted polygraph and other scientific tests to establish his motive and verify his claims. The court had earlier remanded Shwetha to judicial custody on July 10 after the end of her police custody. She has, meanwhile, sought a pardon and offered to confess.

Kenneth has allegedly told investigators that the idea of killing the family first surfaced over a “trivial grievance”. Over the following six months, guided in part by the AI tool, he grew consumed by it, sources said.

“He was planning on starting a cloud kitchen and built a furnace for this purpose. When the murder thought entered his head, he consulted the AI tool, which indicated the merits and demerits of incinerating the bodies before disposal. He had planned to repurpose the furnace he built for burning the bodies after the murder,” police sources said.

Kenneth allegedly told police that he built the iron furnace himself. “He consulted the AI tool all along the course of planning the murder. If he had spoken to a human friend, they may have advised him against the wrong course he had taken,” police said.

“The thought got into his head to ‘eliminate’ the family of his live-in partner, and he got obsessed with it. For six months, he was consumed by this,” police sources said. The impulse is alleged to have been triggered by Shwetha’s grievance against her mother for being “controlling”—and by fears that the mother would ask for Rs 50 lakh Swetha had allegedly borrowed and spent on Kenneth, sources said.

While Kenneth and Shwetha allegedly acted in tandem, the bulk of the planning and execution was Kenneth’s, police sources said.

Kenneth and Shwetha hail from well-to-do middle-class Bengaluru families. Kenneth’s father worked at a major PSU involved in aircraft manufacturing while Shwetha’s father was employed with a global IT company.

Shwetha worked for a while in Bengaluru’s IT sector after graduating but lost it after being allegedly influenced by Kenneth, sources said. Police sources described their relationship as a transactional friendship in which she funded his lifestyle.

On June 22, Shwetha’s mother was allegedly lured to the K R Puram apartment first. Once inside, Kenneth allegedly stabbed her 26 times. When Shwetha’s father and sister arrived a short while later, they were also allegedly stabbed.

After the murders, Kenneth and Shwetha went to Shwetha’s parents’ house to allegedly steal money and silver ornaments, and are alleged to have thrown her younger sister’s mobile phone near the parents’ home. They then fled to Puducherry. “They had gone to Puducherry around 15 days prior to the murder for a holiday as well,” sources said.

Key evidence includes the dying declaration of Somasundar, who was found around 9 pm on June 22 in a pool of blood with multiple stab wounds on a staircase at the Sai Green apartment complex where Shwetha lived. He told police he had been stabbed by his daughter and Kenneth. “My younger daughter Supriya and my wife Muthulakshmi are still in the apartment. Please rescue them,” Somasundar said, according to the FIR, before he was taken to hospital, where he died.

Bengaluru Police allege the accused in a triple murder consulted an AI chatbot for six months while planning the killings, and have sought his chat logs.

SHARE

In what police are describing as India’s first case of its kind, investigators in Bengaluru say a 25-year-old accused in a triple murder consulted an AI chatbot at nearly every stage of a six-month plan to kill his live-in partner’s parents and sister, and have now written to the AI’s parent company seeking his complete chat history as evidence.

### A Family Killed in Seegehalli

The murders took place on June 22 at a rented apartment in Bengaluru’s Seegehalli area, within the K.R. Puram police station’s jurisdiction, where Somasundar, 52, his wife Muthulakshmi, 48, and their younger daughter Supriya, 19, were found stabbed to death. Days later, police arrested the couple’s elder daughter Shweta, 24, and her live-in partner Kenneth, 25, both engineers by profession, after tracking them to Puducherry, where they had gone into hiding.

Investigators say that while both accused acted in tandem, Kenneth was responsible for the bulk of the planning and execution, and it is his alleged reliance on an AI chatbot, reportedly Google Gemini, that has drawn the case unusual attention. Police say he consulted the chatbot repeatedly over roughly six months, seeking guidance at various stages of the alleged conspiracy.

### How Investigators Say the Chatbot Was Used

According to police, Kenneth avoided asking the chatbot direct questions about committing murder or disposing of a body. Instead, investigators allege he framed his queries as hypothetical scenarios, of the kind, “if something like this happens, what should someone do,” a pattern police believe was a deliberate attempt to extract relevant information without triggering the safety mechanisms most AI systems have built in for such requests.

Police say the resulting conversations touched on planning the killings, destroying evidence, removing bloodstains, and evaluating whether an iron furnace Kenneth had built for a planned cloud kitchen business could be repurposed for body disposal. A senior officer told The Indian Express that investigators had “almost considered naming the AI chatbot as an accomplice,” given the extent to which Kenneth appeared to rely on it, though police have been clear that they are not attributing any legal liability to the AI tool itself. Bengaluru Police have formally written to Google seeking the underlying chat logs to corroborate Kenneth’s own account, given during interrogation, of how heavily he depended on the chatbot throughout the planning period.

### Financial Strain and Family Conflict at the Core

The alleged motive traces back to money and mounting family tension. Police say Shweta had borrowed around ₹50 lakh from her mother to fund Kenneth’s cloud kitchen venture, a business that investigators believe failed to generate meaningful returns, leaving the loan largely unpaid even as pressure to repay it grew. Kenneth reportedly told police during interrogation that it was ultimately a “trivial” dispute that pushed him toward the killings, though the underlying pressure had clearly been building for months.

Investigators say Shweta had separately expressed frustration with what she considered her mother’s controlling behaviour, a friction that had reportedly strained the family for some time, while psychological assessments during the probe found Kenneth had become severely socially isolated, relying almost entirely on Shweta for both emotional and financial support after leaving the IT sector.

### What the Case Signals for AI Oversight

The episode has reopened debate around the safeguards built into mainstream AI platforms, which are generally designed to refuse or limit assistance connected to violent or illegal acts. Cybersecurity experts note that the case, if the allegations hold up, appears to illustrate how such safeguards can potentially be circumvented through indirect or hypothetical framing rather than explicit requests, a gap that developers of AI systems have been working to close as these tools see wider adoption.

Renowned cybercrime expert and former IPS officer Prof Triveni Singh said the case underscores how emerging technologies can be misused when combined with clear criminal intent, even as the same tools deliver genuine value across productivity, research, healthcare and education. He said AI cannot replace human judgment or legal accountability, and noted that digital evidence, spanning chat records, cloud data, device forensics and online activity logs, is becoming an increasingly central pillar of modern criminal investigations, one police forces across India will likely need to build far greater technical capacity to handle.

Police say the investigation remains ongoing as they await a formal response from Google and continue forensic verification of the digital evidence, with the precise role each accused played still being established before final charges are framed.

Bengaluru police investigating a triple murder in the city found that one of the accused allegedly used a popular artificial intelligence (AI) chatbot over several months to plan the crime, including seeking information on methods of killing, disposing of bodies and removing bloodstains. The police have sought the accused's chat records from the chatbot's parent company as part of the digital evidence in the case, according to The Indian Express.

The accused, 25-year-old engineer Kenneth, and his live-in partner, Shwetha Somasundar (25), were arrested by the KR Puram police for the alleged murders of Shwetha's mother, Muthulakshmi S. (48), father, Somasundar (54), and younger sister, Supriya (20). The three were allegedly killed at the couple's apartment in K R Puram on June 22.

According to The Indian Express, Kenneth allegedly consulted the AI chatbot over nearly six months while planning the murders. Police said they have written to the chatbot's parent company seeking complete logs of his conversations to corroborate other digital evidence collected during the investigation.

During interrogation, Kenneth allegedly told police that the idea of disposing of the bodies using an iron furnace came after consulting the AI tool. Police said Kenneth had built the furnace as part of plans to start a cloud kitchen but later considered using it for disposal of the bodies.

"He was planning to start a cloud kitchen and had built an iron furnace for this purpose. When the idea of murder came up, he consulted the AI tool, which indicated the merits and demerits of incinerating bodies before disposal. He planned to repurpose the furnace," a police source said.

Police said the alleged motive behind the murders appears to be linked to financial disputes and strained family relations. Police sources said both accused come from middle-class families. Kenneth's father is a retired employee of a defence public sector undertaking involved in aircraft manufacturing, while Shwetha's late father worked for a multinational IT company.

Investigators said psychological assessments conducted during the probe pointed to severe social isolation. According to police, Shwetha had earlier worked in a high-paying role at a multinational social media company but lost her job after becoming increasingly dependent on Kenneth.

Police described their relationship as transactional, alleging that Shwetha financially supported Kenneth while he remained socially isolated from friends and family.

**Background of the case**

On June 22, police alleged, Muthulakshmi was lured to the K R Puram apartment, where Kenneth stabbed her 26 times. When Shwetha's father and younger sister arrived separately a short while later, they too were allegedly attacked and killed.

After the murders, the couple allegedly travelled to Shwetha's parental home in southeast Bengaluru and stole cash and silver ornaments before fleeing to Puducherry. Police said they had also travelled to Puducherry on vacation about two weeks before the killings.

The investigation gathered momentum after Somasundar, despite sustaining fatal injuries, managed to crawl out of the apartment. Neighbours found him on the staircase around 9 pm. Before succumbing to his injuries, he reportedly gave a dying declaration identifying his daughter Shwetha and Kenneth as the attackers and urged police to rescue his wife and younger daughter, who remained inside the flat.

Shwetha was arrested in Puducherry on June 24, while Kenneth was arrested within the following two days.

Shwetha was remanded to judicial custody on July 10 after the completion of her police custody. Police said she has expressed willingness to make a confessional statement in exchange for a pardon. Kenneth, who underwent polygraph and other scientific examinations during nine days of police custody, was remanded to judicial custody by a Bengaluru magistrate court on Saturday, July 18.

# How To Poison Someone, Burn Body: Bengaluru Man Asks AI Before Triple Murders



## Investigators found that the accused had used Google Gemini to create hypothetical scenarios and seek information related to committing crimes.




Read Time: 3 mins

Police also alleged that the accused had planned to destroy evidence.

* The accused in the Bengaluru murder case used AI to research weapons, poisoning, and body disposal methods
* Police found he planned to burn the body using furnace equipment for evidence destruction
* The accused attacked the mother first, then stabbed the father and sister during the assault

The prime accused in the Bengaluru triple murder case allegedly used Google's AI chatbot Gemini to research weapons, body disposal, poisoning and ways to evade police detection while planning the crime, according to Whitefield Division Deputy Commissioner of Police (DCP) Saidulu Adavath.

Speaking to NDTV, DCP Adavath said investigators found that the accused had used Google Gemini to create hypothetical scenarios and seek information related to committing crimes. The scenarios included "What if people come to my house?", "How do I attack them?"

“He was using Google Gemini. He created hypothetical situations and searched for information about weapons, how to burn a body, how to stay without using a mobile phone and similar topics. He even sought details on different types of weapons and how slow poisoning works,” he said.

Police also alleged that the accused had planned to destroy evidence by setting up a furnace.

“He wanted to start a cloud kitchen. He had procured equipment, including a furnace and a tank, and had set them up. The plan was to use them to dispose of the body,” the DCP said.

Explaining the sequence of the killings, Adavath said investigators believe the accused first attacked the mother before assaulting the other family members.

“The mother was attacked first. By then, the father and sister came to the door. He stabbed the father. When the sister raised an alarm, he turned towards her and stabbed her as well. She collapsed, while the father managed to run downstairs despite sustaining stab injuries,” he said.

Speaking about the role of the accused's partner, the officer said she was allegedly aware of the conspiracy.

“She was present and was aware of what was happening. She knew about the planning,” he said.

On the alleged motive, Adavath said the accused told investigators that financial problems and pressure from the woman's family had contributed to the crime.

“The accused told us he had used the girl's money. She also did not want to return to her family and disliked them. They were under pressure from her family and, according to the accused, that was one of the reasons behind the crime,” he said.

Police are now following the legal process to obtain the accused's search history from Google.

“We believe a request has already been sent to Google. It requires a legal process, and the necessary application has to be made through proper legal channels,” the DCP said.

The accused's electronic devices have also been seized and sent for forensic examination.

“We do not have screenshots of the chats. The devices have been seized and sent for forensic examination,” Adavath said.

* By: Express News Service

In a chilling revelation in the Bengaluru triple murder investigation, the police have discovered that a 25-year-old engineer, Kenneth, repeatedly consulted a popular search engine’s artificial intelligence (AI) tool to plan the execution and cover-up of his live-in partner’s family.

Kenneth and his partner, Shwetha Somasundar, 25, were arrested by the K R Puram police for the brutal murders of Shwetha’s mother Muthulakshmi S, 48, father Somasundar, 54, and younger sister Supriya. 20. **The killings took place on the evening of June 22** at the K R Puram apartment complex where the couple lived together.

Story continues below this ad

According to police sources familiar with the probe, the AI tool acted as a roadmap over six months of meticulous planning, leading investigators to consider it an “accomplice” in the crime. The investigation has also spotlighted the dark side of severe social isolation among tech-immersed youth who lack real-world support systems.

## Repurposing a cloud kitchen furnace

As per police sources, **Kenneth confessed during the interrogation** that the idea of the murder stemmed from a trivial grievance.





“He was planning on starting a cloud kitchen and built an iron furnace for this purpose. When the murder thought entered his head, he consulted the AI tool, which indicated the merits and demerits of incinerating bodies before disposal. He planned to repurpose that furnace to burn the bodies after the murders,” a police source said.

Story continues below this ad

The police noted that the lack of human interaction facilitated the crime. “He consulted the AI tool all along the course of planning the murder. If he had spoken to a human friend, they may have advised him against the dangerous course he had taken,” the police source added.

Kenneth allegedly consulted the AI tool for advice on the method of killing three people, chemicals to be used to get rid of blood stains, packaging of the bodies after the murder, and moving them from the apartment he shared with Shwetha.

The Bengaluru police have written to the parent tech company of the AI tool, requesting complete logs of Kenneth’s chat histories to substantiate the digital evidence for the prosecution.

Story continues below this ad

## Resentment towards mother

Police sources said the motive behind the killings appears to be rooted in financial strain and domestic resentment. Shwetha reportedly held deep animosity toward her mother for being “controlling”. Also, she feared being forced to return Rs 50 lakh that she had borrowed from her mother and subsequently squandered on Kenneth’s lifestyle.

On June 22, Shwetha’s mother Muthulakshmi was allegedly lured to the K R Puram apartment first. Once inside, Kenneth allegedly stabbed her 26 times. When Shwetha’s father and sister arrived at the flat a short time later, they were also allegedly stabbed.

Following the attack, the couple allegedly travelled to Shwetha’s parental home in southeast Bengaluru to steal cash and silver ornaments. They discarded her younger sister’s mobile phone near the scene before fleeing to Puducherry for a brief getaway, said the police.

Story continues below this ad

“They had gone to Puducherry around 15 days before the murder for a holiday as well,” sources said.

Shwetha’s father Somasundar managed to crawl out of the flat. At around 9 pm on June 22, neighbours found him lying in a pool of blood on the staircase of the Sai Green apartment complex. Before succumbing to injuries at the hospital, Somasundar gave a crucial dying declaration to responding police officers. He stated that he had been attacked by his daughter Shwetha and her friend Kenneth, and begged officers to rescue his wife and younger daughter who were still trapped inside the flat.

The police arrested Shwetha from Puducheery on June 24 and Kenneth within the next two days.

## Social isolation and judicial custody

Both accused hail from well-to-do, middle-class families of first-generation migrants in Bengaluru. Kenneth’s father is a retired employee of a major defence public sector undertaking involved in aircraft manufacturing, while Shwetha’s late father worked for a global IT firm. Kenneth’s father has since completely distanced himself from the case, telling his son to handle the legal consequences alone.

Story continues below this ad

Police sources said psychological evaluations during the probe highlighted deep social isolation. Shwetha, who previously held a high-paying job at a multinational social media news forum, lost her job after becoming heavily dependent on Kenneth.

Police sources described their relationship as a transactional friendship in which she funded his lifestyle and he was completely cut off from other friends. The police added that the two displayed a lack of social responsibility, processing real-world consequences as if they were playing a video game.

Following the conclusion of her police custody, Shwetha was remanded to judicial custody on July 10, where she has reportedly **offered to make a full confession statement** in exchange for a pardon. Kenneth, who underwent polygraph and scientific testing during his nine days in police custody, was formally remanded to judicial custody by a Bengaluru magistrate court on Saturday.

# Triple Murder: Police Seek AI Chat Logs After Probe Reveals Accused Used Chatbot To Plan Killings

## The murders were reported on June 22 this year at apartment where Somasundar, his wife Muthulaxmi, and their younger daughter were found stabbed to death.

Representational Image (IANS)

By  PTI

Published : July 21, 2026 at 2:57 PM IST

3 Min Read

**Bengaluru:**The Bengaluru Police have written to an AI tool company seeking details of chat history after the investigation into the recent triple murder case revealed that the prime accused used the assistance of an AI chatbot to execute the murders, which he had been planning for nearly six months, officials said on Tuesday.

The murders were reported on June 22 this year at an apartment in Seegehalli under the limits of K R Puram Police Station, where Somasundar (52), his wife Muthulaxmi (48), and their younger daughter Supriya (19) were found stabbed to death.

Days after the murders, the deceased couple's elder daughter Shwetha (24) and her live-in partner Kenneth (25), who fled the spot after committing the crime, were arrested separately from Puducherry, where they had been taking shelter to evade arrest, police said.

The investigation revealed that the alleged motive behind the murders appeared to be financial disputes and strained family relations, with Shwetha harbouring grievances against her mother for being "controlling", they said.

According to police, Shwetha had allegedly borrowed Rs 50 lakh from her mother, Muthulaxmi, for Kenneth to start a cloud kitchen business. The money was spent, and she feared how it would be repaid.

While Kenneth and Shwetha allegedly acted in tandem, the entire planning and execution of the murders were carried out by Kenneth, who consulted an AI chatbot at every stage, including seeking information on how to kill, dispose of bodies, removing bloodstains, and whether the furnace built by him for the planned cloud kitchen business here could be repurposed to incinerate the bodies, a senior police officer said.

During interrogation, Kenneth confessed to police that a trivial issue had triggered him to eliminate Shwetha's family members. He also admitted that he depended heavily on the AI chatbot for guidance throughout the six months of planning the murders, the officer said, adding that it had acted as an accomplice in the crime.

Following the detailed interrogation, the officer said investigators have written to the parent AI company seeking digital evidence of Kenneth's chat history with the AI tool to corroborate his version.

Meanwhile, psychological assessments conducted during the probe revealed that Kenneth suffered from severe social isolation. Police alleged that Shwetha financially supported Kenneth while he remained socially isolated from friends and family.

Police said Shwetha had earlier worked in the IT sector but lost her job after allegedly becoming increasingly influenced by Kenneth.

After the murders, the accused duo allegedly went to Shwetha's house, from where they stole cash and silver ornaments before fleeing to Puducherry, they said. Police said that after luring Muthulaxmi to their apartment on June 22, Kenneth stabbed her multiple times. Subsequently, when her husband and younger daughter arrived, they too were stabbed.

Somasundar somehow managed to reach the staircase despite suffering grievous injuries. He was noticed by neighbours, who alerted the police. In his dying declaration, Somasundar told police that he had been stabbed by his daughter and her live-in partner and urged them to rescue his wife and younger daughter before he was taken to hospital, where he later died, they added.

# How to kill, clean, and move bodies: Techie’s prompts reveal AI ‘accomplice’ in Bengaluru triple murder

## The police said that Kenneth and Shwetha's extreme isolation bred an "eliminate them" mindset detached from real-world consequences.

By: Express News Service

5 min read*Bengaluru*Jul 19, 2026 10:29 AM IST

Shwetha was arrested in Puducherry on June 24, two days after the murders of her parents and sister, and Kenneth within the next two days (Express photo/Special arrangement).

In a chilling revelation in the Bengaluru triple murder investigation, the police have discovered that a 25-year-old engineer, Kenneth, repeatedly consulted a popular search engine’s artificial intelligence (AI) tool to plan the execution and cover-up of his live-in partner’s family.

Kenneth and his partner, Shwetha Somasundar, 25, were arrested by the K R Puram police for the brutal murders of Shwetha’s mother Muthulakshmi S, 48, father Somasundar, 54, and younger sister Supriya. 20. **The killings took place on the evening of June 22** at the K R Puram apartment complex where the couple lived together.

According to police sources familiar with the probe, the AI tool acted as a roadmap over six months of meticulous planning, leading investigators to consider it an “accomplice” in the crime. The investigation has also spotlighted the dark side of severe social isolation among tech-immersed youth who lack real-world support systems.

## Repurposing a cloud kitchen furnace

As per police sources, **Kenneth confessed during the interrogation** that the idea of the murder stemmed from a trivial grievance.

“He was planning on starting a cloud kitchen and built an iron furnace for this purpose. When the murder thought entered his head, he consulted the AI tool, which indicated the merits and demerits of incinerating bodies before disposal. He planned to repurpose that furnace to burn the bodies after the murders,” a police source said.

The police noted that the lack of human interaction facilitated the crime. “He consulted the AI tool all along the course of planning the murder. If he had spoken to a human friend, they may have advised him against the dangerous course he had taken,” the police source added.

Kenneth allegedly consulted the AI tool for advice on the method of killing three people, chemicals to be used to get rid of blood stains, packaging of the bodies after the murder, and moving them from the apartment he shared with Shwetha.

Story continues below this ad

The Bengaluru police have written to the parent tech company of the AI tool, requesting complete logs of Kenneth’s chat histories to substantiate the digital evidence for the prosecution.

## Resentment towards mother

Police sources said the motive behind the killings appears to be rooted in financial strain and domestic resentment. Shwetha reportedly held deep animosity toward her mother for being “controlling”. Also, she feared being forced to return Rs 50 lakh that she had borrowed from her mother and subsequently squandered on Kenneth’s lifestyle.

On June 22, Shwetha’s mother Muthulakshmi was allegedly lured to the K R Puram apartment first. Once inside, Kenneth allegedly stabbed her 26 times. When Shwetha’s father and sister arrived at the flat a short time later, they were also allegedly stabbed.

Following the attack, the couple allegedly travelled to Shwetha’s parental home in southeast Bengaluru to steal cash and silver ornaments. They discarded her younger sister’s mobile phone near the scene before fleeing to Puducherry for a brief getaway, said the police.

Story continues below this ad

“They had gone to Puducherry around 15 days before the murder for a holiday as well,” sources said.

Shwetha’s father Somasundar managed to crawl out of the flat. At around 9 pm on June 22, neighbours found him lying in a pool of blood on the staircase of the Sai Green apartment complex. Before succumbing to injuries at the hospital, Somasundar gave a crucial dying declaration to responding police officers. He stated that he had been attacked by his daughter Shwetha and her friend Kenneth, and begged officers to rescue his wife and younger daughter who were still trapped inside the flat.

The police arrested Shwetha from Puducheery on June 24 and Kenneth within the next two days.

## Social isolation and judicial custody

Both accused hail from well-to-do, middle-class families of first-generation migrants in Bengaluru. Kenneth’s father is a retired employee of a major defence public sector undertaking involved in aircraft manufacturing, while Shwetha’s late father worked for a global IT firm. Kenneth’s father has since completely distanced himself from the case, telling his son to handle the legal consequences alone.

Story continues below this ad

Police sources said psychological evaluations during the probe highlighted deep social isolation. Shwetha, who previously held a high-paying job at a multinational social media news forum, lost her job after becoming heavily dependent on Kenneth.

Police sources described their relationship as a transactional friendship in which she funded his lifestyle and he was completely cut off from other friends. The police added that the two displayed a lack of social responsibility, processing real-world consequences as if they were playing a video game.

Following the conclusion of her police custody, Shwetha was remanded to judicial custody on July 10, where she has reportedly **offered to make a full confession statement** in exchange for a pardon. Kenneth, who underwent polygraph and scientific testing during his nine days in police custody, was formally remanded to judicial custody by a Bengaluru magistrate court on Saturday.

# Bengaluru accused used Google Gemini to plan 3 murders, he is not alone in seeking deadly advice from AI

## Kenneth Arun Kumar reportedly used Google Gemini to plan murder of three people. As AI enters our lives, increasingly people are asking ChatGPT, Gemini and Claude for deadly advice and in some cases are even receiving "helpful" tips from the AI tools.

Advertisement

Bengaluru Police allege the triple murder accused spent six months using Google Gemini to plan the killings.

Divya Bhati

New Delhi,UPDATED: Jul 22, 2026 13:44 IST

AI chatbots like ChatGPT, Gemini, Claude and Grok can answer almost anything. Need recipe ideas? Ask AI. Need help writing code? Ask AI. But as it turns out, some people are turning to AI for something far more sinister. From mass shootings to cold-blooded murders, AI is increasingly showing up as a tool that many people are using while planning violent crimes. And in some cases, they are even getting the answers back with AI tools trying to be “helpful” in whatever their users are trying to do.

advertisement

❮❯

The latest example comes from Bengaluru, where cops claim that 25-year-old Kenneth spent nearly six months consulting Google's Gemini before allegedly murdering his live-in partner's parents and younger sister. Investigators claim he used the chatbot to gather information on killing methods, removing bloodstains, disposing of bodies and even whether an iron furnace could be used to destroy evidence.

But don't AI chatbots have guardrails? They do. So how does someone get around them? Well, they are tricking the AI bot.

Police believe Kenneth allegedly avoided asking direct questions such as, "How do I commit murder?" Instead, he framed his prompts as hypothetical scenarios, asking what someone should do "if something like this happens". Investigators say that helped him gather information without triggering obvious safety filters.

Cops also allege that he initially considered disposing of the bodies in an iron furnace built for his proposed cloud kitchen business before abandoning the idea after evaluating its practicality with Gemini.

Police have now reportedly sought access to his Gemini chat history as part of the investigation. India Today Tech has reached out to Google for a comment and we will update the copy if and when we receive inputs.

Note that the allegations are yet to be tested in court. However, the Bengaluru case is far from an isolated incident. From the US to Australia, investigators have uncovered several cases in which suspects allegedly turned to AI chatbots to research attacks, refine violent plans or obtain tactical information before committing crimes.

### 2025 Florida State University mass shooting

One of the recent international cases that came into light due to AI connection is the 2025 Florida State University mass shooting.

According to a lawsuit filed by the family of one of the victims, the alleged shooter exchanged hundreds of conversations with ChatGPT in the months leading up to the attack. The lawsuit claims the chatbot provided planning-related information, while prosecutors later reviewed the chat logs as part of the investigation. Florida's Attorney General also launched a criminal investigation into ChatGPT's role.

OpenAI, however, rejected the allegations, saying ChatGPT only returned publicly available factual information and did not encourage or promote violence.

### Teen allegedly used AI to plan mass shooting in Australia

advertisement

The US isn’t the only place where AI allegedly has became part of a criminal investigation in a case.

In Australia, court documents claim a 13-year-old repeatedly used generative AI to create detailed mass shooting scenarios, draft violent manifestos and even requested a story describing a "Bondi-style" beach massacre. The alleged target was a school, but police arrested the teenager before any attack could take place.

The case also became one of the earliest examples of AI-generated conversations being used as evidence in an alleged terrorism-style investigation.

### 2025 Cybertruck explosion in the US

Another case that caught global attention due to AI connection was the 2025 Cybertruck explosion outside the Trump International Hotel in Las Vegas. According to a report by The Guardian, investigators revealed former US Army soldier Matthew Livelsberger used ChatGPT to research explosives and tactical information before carrying out the attack.

### Teen stabs 3 girls in Finland

In another case, this time from Finland, a 16-year-old allegedly spent months planning an attack on his school, using a chatbot to help draft a manifesto and prepare for the assault. He later stabbed three teenage girls at a school in Pirkkala. Police said they examined the alleged AI-assisted manifesto as part of their investigation, with the suspect reportedly claiming he had planned the attack for around six months.

advertisement

### The danger of easy access to AI

Of course, AI is making everyday life easier for millions of people. It helps students study, developers write code, businesses automate routine work and professionals get more done in less time. But like any powerful technology, it is only as good as the intent of the person using it.

With AI now just a few clicks away for almost anyone with an internet connection, the ease of access is becoming a growing concern for technology companies and law enforcement agencies alike.

To mitigate the risks, AI companies have introduced stricter guardrails designed to stop chatbots from providing harmful information. But as the Bengaluru case and several others suggest, those guardrails aren't foolproof. Some users are finding ways around them by disguising dangerous requests as hypothetical scenarios. And many times, as smart as AI is, it is getting fooled by the intents of its human users.

Case records show the sequence of events came to a head on June 25, when Bengaluru police arrested Kenneth (25) and his live-in partner Shwetha, both engineering graduates who had been planning to start a business, for allegedly killing her mother Muthulakshmi S (48), sister Supriya (20) and father Somasundar (54), in that order, at their flat in K R Puram three days earlier. The alleged motive, according to case records: a dispute over money Shwetha had taken from her parents to spend on her partner.





This is possibly the first time Bengaluru police have encountered such extensive use of an AI tool in the planning and execution of a murder, sources familiar with the probe said. The tool allegedly shaped Kenneth’s thinking at every stage and had a significant bearing on how the crime was planned, they said.

Advertisement

So much so, as part of the investigation, police have written to the AI tool’s makers seeking details of Kenneth’s interactions with it, to corroborate the digital evidence in the case.

For investigators, the case also points to the social isolation of a tech-savvy generation immersed in the information and entertainment served up by their devices. “The girl did not have any friend, male or female, other than Kenneth from her college days. Kenneth had a girlfriend earlier who left him because she suspected him of lying and stealing,” sources said.

Kenneth’s alleged inability to reflect on the consequences of his actions, a lack of social responsibility, and a rapid build-up of frustration that led to an “eliminate them” mindset, “as though life were a video game”, were among the other factors behind the crime, police sources said.

Last Saturday, a magistrate’s court remanded Kenneth to judicial custody after nine days in police custody, during which police conducted polygraph and other scientific tests to establish his motive and verify his claims. The court had earlier remanded Shwetha to judicial custody on July 10 after the end of her police custody. She has, meanwhile, sought a pardon and offered to confess.

Kenneth has allegedly told investigators that the idea of killing the family first surfaced over a “trivial grievance”. Over the following six months, guided in part by the AI tool, he grew consumed by it, sources said.

“He was planning on starting a cloud kitchen and built a furnace for this purpose. When the murder thought entered his head, he consulted the AI tool, which indicated the merits and demerits of incinerating the bodies before disposal. He had planned to repurpose the furnace he built for burning the bodies after the murder,” police sources said.

Kenneth allegedly told police that he built the iron furnace himself. “He consulted the AI tool all along the course of planning the murder. If he had spoken to a human friend, they may have advised him against the wrong course he had taken,” police said.

“The thought got into his head to ‘eliminate’ the family of his live-in partner, and he got obsessed with it. For six months, he was consumed by this,” police sources said. The impulse is alleged to have been triggered by Shwetha’s grievance against her mother for being “controlling”—and by fears that the mother would ask for Rs 50 lakh Swetha had allegedly borrowed and spent on Kenneth, sources said.

While Kenneth and Shwetha allegedly acted in tandem, the bulk of the planning and execution was Kenneth’s, police sources said.

Kenneth and Shwetha hail from well-to-do middle-class Bengaluru families. Kenneth’s father worked at a major PSU involved in aircraft manufacturing while Shwetha’s father was employed with a global IT company.

Shwetha worked for a while in Bengaluru’s IT sector after graduating but lost it after being allegedly influenced by Kenneth, sources said. Police sources described their relationship as a transactional friendship in which she funded his lifestyle.

On June 22, Shwetha’s mother was allegedly lured to the K R Puram apartment first. Once inside, Kenneth allegedly stabbed her 26 times. When Shwetha’s father and sister arrived a short while later, they were also allegedly stabbed.

After the murders, Kenneth and Shwetha went to Shwetha’s parents’ house to allegedly steal money and silver ornaments, and are alleged to have thrown her younger sister’s mobile phone near the parents’ home. They then fled to Puducherry. “They had gone to Puducherry around 15 days prior to the murder for a holiday as well,” sources said.

Key evidence includes the dying declaration of Somasundar, who was found around 9 pm on June 22 in a pool of blood with multiple stab wounds on a staircase at the Sai Green apartment complex where Shwetha lived. He told police he had been stabbed by his daughter and Kenneth. “My younger daughter Supriya and my wife Muthulakshmi are still in the apartment. Please rescue them,” Somasundar said, according to the FIR, before he was taken to hospital, where he died.

## Software professional Kenneth Arun Kumar and his live-in partner Shwetha were arrested for the brutal stabbing of Shwetha's mother, father, and younger sister

In one of the most chilling cases of technology-assisted crime in India, Bengaluru Police investigating a gruesome triple murder revealed that the primary accused spent nearly six months consulting an artificial intelligence (AI) chatbot to plan every detail of the crime. The level of reliance was so extensive that senior investigators remarked that the AI tool effectively functioned as a “confidant" and an “accomplice" throughout the conspiracy.

The accused, 25-year-old software professional Kenneth Arun Kumar, along with his live-in partner Shwetha, was arrested for the brutal stabbing of Shwetha’s mother, father, and younger sister at an apartment in the city’s KR Puram area.

## **Bypassing Safety Filters with Hypothetical Prompts**

According to police, Kenneth turned to the AI chatbot to guide his decisions after financial disputes over an unpaid Rs 50 lakh loan escalated. Sufferers of severe social isolation, the couple relied entirely on digital interactions rather than human counsel.

Rather than asking explicit questions that would trigger safety blocks—such as “how to commit a murder"—Kenneth allegedly framed his queries as hypothetical scenarios.

Key areas where the AI was queried included:

* Attack Tactics: Framing scenarios like defending against home intruders to learn how to blind and incapacitate victims.
* Evidence Elimination: Seeking advice on specific chemical agents to erase bloodstains.
* Body Disposal: Inquiring about methods to package bodies and evaluating whether an iron furnace built for a proposed cloud kitchen venture could incinerate human remains.

## **Why Cops View the Chatbot as a Digital Confidant**

While the police have not suggested that the AI tool bears direct legal liability, officers noted that the software filled the role a co-conspirator normally would. By providing continuous, non-judgmental answers to reframed questions, the chatbot inadvertently helped refine an abstract criminal thought into an actionable six-month execution plan.

Investigators have written to the parent technology firm to secure complete chat logs to corroborate digital evidence for the prosecution. The case stands as a landmark warning regarding the dark side of severe digital immersion and the evolving challenges of AI guardrails in criminal investigations.
